name: Fluency and Reading Supports
title: Fluency and Reading Supports
answer: Fluency and reading supports use speech tools to give students access to text, either by listening to a student read aloud and marking missed or slow words, or by reading content aloud with highlighting, syllable breaks and definitions. They matter because they can keep a student with a reading disability learning at grade level in every subject, but the same support can remove the very practice a reading lesson is meant to build, so the decision belongs to the teacher and the individualized education program team.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: Fluency and reading supports are speech based tools that help students work with text they cannot yet read fluently on their own. For younger readers, a tool can listen as a student reads aloud and flag the words that were missed or read slowly, giving the teacher a picture of where fluency is breaking down. For older students who struggle with print, supports such as Microsoft Immersive Reader and Read&Write by Texthelp can read text aloud, highlight words as they are spoken, split words into syllables and define unfamiliar terms. The problem these tools solve is access: a student with a reading disability can use them to learn science or history at grade level instead of falling behind in every subject, not just reading. The open question is not whether the tools work but when a support helps and when it removes practice the student needs.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the younger grades, a student reads aloud while the speech tool listens and marks words that were missed or read slowly, which gives the teacher a record of fluency to work from. The book notes that these tools struggle with young voices, so the teacher should listen as well rather than relying on the tool alone. For older students who struggle with print, reading supports are used across content areas: the tool reads text aloud, highlights words as they are spoken, breaks words into syllables and defines unfamiliar terms, so a student with a reading disability can keep up with grade level science or history. The choice of when to use a support depends on the lesson. In a history lesson, text to speech may be exactly right, while in a reading lesson the same support might skip the practice the student most needs, and the individualized education program team decides which applies when.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea's evidence base as mixed. It reports that a large study found strong reading gains from an AI reading platform used by regular teachers, but notes that the study's authors were connected to the company, so districts should confirm the results locally (Srinivasan & Murthy, 2021). The book also states that these tools struggle with young voices, which is why a teacher should listen too. No other study, figure or finding is given for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that a support can get in the way as easily as it helps. The book describes the goal as strategic offloading, where the tool handles the part of the task that blocks access while the student still builds the skill that matters for that lesson. That means the same text to speech support that is right for a history lesson may be wrong for a reading lesson, because it skips the practice the student most needs. The individualized education program team should decide which applies when, and the teacher should listen to young readers rather than trusting the tool's judgment of their voices. These decisions stay with people, not with the software.
